language.note: Malay is the official language, while Brunei Malay is the everyday spoken variety. Rumi is widely used, and Jawi remains official for institutional names and signage.

culture_note: Brunei keeps the Jawi script alongside the Latin Rumi alphabet. Ministry names and street signs are often written in both scripts, because Jawi is seen as guarding the country's Malay-Islamic identity.
people_note: When greeting, Bruneians give a light handshake and then touch the chest with the right hand; they point with the thumb, not the index finger. Guests remove their shoes at home and greet the eldest first.

story.text: At Kampong Ayer, wooden houses stand on stilts above the Brunei River. A guest arrives by boat, removes his shoes at the steps, and greets the eldest person in the house first. His greeting is brief: "Salam" or "Assalamualaikum". After a light handshake, he touches his right palm to his chest as a sign of respect. The official language of Brunei is Malay, but in daily conversation people speak the Brunei Malay variety. The relationship between the two is called diglossia: standard Malay is used in schools and official ceremonies, while Brunei Malay serves as the lingua franca of markets and homes. The country also keeps the Jawi script alongside the Latin Rumi alphabet. Ministry names and street signs are often written twice, once in Rumi and once in Jawi. To point at something, Bruneians use the thumb with the other fingers folded, never the index finger. When food is served, guests are encouraged to taste a little so the host does not feel refused.

language.note: Khmer is the official language of Cambodia and is a non-tonal language. Its polite register borrows heavily from Pali and Sanskrit.

culture_note: Cambodians greet with the sompeah, both palms pressed together in front of the chest. The height of the hands follows the status of the person greeted, because the gesture expresses the level of respect.
people_note: Younger people greet first, and objects are given or received with the right hand. Touching another person's head is considered rude, and women should avoid sitting too close to a monk.

story.text: In front of the gates of Angkor Wat, a guide welcomes a visitor with the sompeah: both palms pressed together in front of the chest, the back slightly bowed. The height of the hands follows the status of the person being greeted. The official language of Cambodia is Khmer, a member of the Austroasiatic family that is not tonal, unlike the tonal languages of its neighbours. Khmer is written in the Khmer script, an abugida descended from the Brahmi script of southern India and used since at least the seventh century. In that script, vowels appear as marks around a consonant, and consonant clusters take a subscript form. The everyday greeting is suostei, while chumreap suor is used with elders or officials. Khmer polite vocabulary borrows heavily from Pali and Sanskrit through the influence of Buddhism and Hinduism. Courtesy toward monks is highly valued: the hands are raised to eyebrow level, and women should avoid touching or sitting too close to a monk.

language.note: Lao is the official language of Laos and is a tonal language. It is related to Thai and has absorbed many words from Pali.

culture_note: Lao people greet with the nop, palms pressed together at chest or chin height. The value of 'sabai', a sense of ease and calm, makes the greeting sabaidee a wish for the other person's well-being as well.
people_note: Younger people or those of lower status greet first. Shoes are removed before entering a home or temple, and no one steps over a person who is sitting or lying down.

story.text: Every morning in Luang Prabang, monks walk in procession to receive offerings of sticky rice from residents. The official language of Laos is Lao, a member of the Kra-Dai family, which is tonal and related to Thai. Lao is written in the Lao script, a rounded and flowing abugida descended from Brahmi. The most common greeting is sabaidee. Literally it means something like 'well and good', since sabai means comfortable or healthy and dee means good. It can be used at any time of day, morning or evening, with anyone. Lao people greet with the nop: both palms pressed together at chest or chin height, accompanied by a nod. Age difference determines how high the hands are held. On entering a home or temple, shoes are removed, and a person does not step over someone who is sitting. Meals are usually shared at a low table, with sticky rice as the staple food, eaten by hand.

The official language of Tajikistan is Tajik, a member of the Indo-European family in the Iranian branch. Tajik is in fact a variety of Persian written in the Cyrillic alphabet since 1940. language.note: The official language of North Korea is Korean. Its standard variety, Munhwao, is based on the Pyongyang dialect and tends to avoid loanwords.

culture_note: Hangul was created in 1443 during the Joseon Dynasty so that ordinary people could read and write. In North Korea the script is called Chosŏn'gŭl and serves as a national symbol of pride.
people_note: Younger people greet their elders first with a bow. Objects are given or received with both hands, and the polite speech register is used with people who are older or of higher status.

story.text: At a school in Pyongyang, pupils greet their teacher with the polite phrase annyeonghasimnikka and a bow. The official language of North Korea is Korean, which its speakers call chosonmal. The standard variety is called Munhwao, 'cultural language', and is based on the Pyongyang dialect. Korean is generally placed in the Koreanic family, though its relation to other families is still debated. The language is written in Hangul, a native script created in 1443 during the Joseon Dynasty so that ordinary people could read and write. In North Korea the script is called Chosŏn'gŭl. Hangul is not an ordinary alphabet but a featural script: the shapes of its consonants imitate the position of the mouth and tongue when the sound is made. To give thanks, North Koreans more often use gomapseumnida, which has a native Korean root, while gamsahamnida, from Sino-Korean, is also understood. The farewell to someone leaving is annyeonghi gasipsio.
